\title{A certified unstable eigenvalue of a columnar model of the front of Hou's Navier-Stokes collapse, and measured non-axisymmetric growth on the collapsing state}
\author{Andrew Mullen\\ Independent researcher\\ \href{mailto:climbtheswissapps@gmail.com}{climbtheswissapps@gmail.com}\\ ORCID: \href{https://orcid.org/0009-0001-8581-4286}{0009-0001-8581-4286}}

\begin{abstract}
Hou's interior scenario is the leading numerical candidate for an interior finite-time singularity of the unforced axisymmetric Navier-Stokes equations, and the viscosity in it is raised by hand at a chosen time in order to suppress a shear instability of the collapsing front. We compute its growth rates, and identify its candidate mechanism in a parallel-flow model of the front. For a parallel-flow (columnar) model of the front -- a degree-30 polynomial fit of one column, carrying an artificial no-slip wall at twice the core radius, which brackets rather than predicts the two-dimensional rate -- we prove, by a computer-assisted argument of Plum's type in verified interval arithmetic, that the continuous columnar operator has an eigenvalue with growth rate at least $\sn{5.0802}{4}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, which is 1.24 times the collapse rate of the state it is taken from: an unstable eigenvalue of a swirling column with axial flow, certified as such, together with local uniqueness of the eigenpair. We also give the first non-axisymmetric stability table for this scenario: growth rates of azimuthal modes $m = 0, 1, 2$ about the Euler and the viscous collapsing state, with a sweep over five viscosities, measured in a norm whose threshold we state as a sufficient condition rather than an equivalence. At Hou's first-stage viscosity every family tested outruns the collapse inside the first eleven percent of the remaining time, the short-wave families of the three azimuthal wavenumbers crossing within half a percentage point of one another, and applying his tenfold viscosity at that state, earlier in the remaining time than his own switch, moves that crossing from 4 to 15 percent without removing it. Nonlinearly, the mode depletes the collapse on the Euler states and, for the one localized seed run, leaves it unchanged to 0.02 percent out to 24 percent of the remaining time and to within 0.15 percent out to 35 percent on the viscous state. We continue Hou's first-stage solution, without his increase of viscosity, to a swirl maximum about 1450 times its initial value on two agreeing grids, and far less resolved to between fifteen and twenty-two thousand times; the measurements are made out to 1216 times. We identify the front as a fed strained layer at the Burgers scale, and measure the part of the Type I hypothesis that has content: the meridional quantities $|r u^r|$ and $|r u^z|$ rather than the full $|u|\,|x'|$, which is pinned from below by a circulation that obeys a maximum principle. We report them in the collapsing core, the global supremum being uninformative because it is attained in an outer flow that is effectively frozen. Over the resolved range the radial one is flat and the axial one rises by 36 percent, non-monotonically; across the late transition at which the one-scale collapse ends they rise by 27 and 60 percent.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The regularity problem for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations remains open in both directions. On the numerical side the strongest evidence for singular behaviour comes from the axisymmetric flows with swirl of Luo and Hou \cite{LH14a,LH14b} at a solid boundary and, in the interior, of Hou \cite{H23a} for Euler and Hou \cite{H23b} for Navier-Stokes. The boundary scenario now has a computer-assisted proof of stable nearly self-similar blowup for Euler \cite{CH25}, whose rigorous-numerics half \cite{CH25b} is the closest computer-assisted precedent in this problem to the certificates below; the interior scenario is supported by a self-similar profile fitted through amplifications of order $10^{7}$ in Euler and, at a viscosity of $\sn{5}{-4}$ raised tenfold at a chosen time, in Navier-Stokes. It is the leading numerical candidate for an interior finite-time singularity of the unforced axisymmetric equations.

Two questions about it have not, to our knowledge, been asked in print. First, every stability statement about these scenarios -- Hou's perturbations of the data, the nonlinear stability of Chen and Hou \cite{CH25}, and the machine-learned profiles of \cite{WLGB23} with the unstable-direction counts of \cite{W25}, those counts being for the one-dimensional Cordoba-Cordoba-Fontelos, two-dimensional porous-media and two-dimensional Boussinesq models rather than for axisymmetric Euler itself, and the stability framework of \cite{DGGA26} for the self-similar Euler profile of \cite{GDA26}, whose perturbations are required to inherit the symmetry of the profile -- is a statement within the axisymmetric class. Whether the collapsing state is stable to symmetry-breaking perturbations is unknown, and the question matters because the viscosity Hou raises by hand is raised precisely to suppress a shear instability of the front \cite[Sec. 3]{H23b}. Second, the viscous scenario's relation to the exclusion theorems for Type I singularities of axisymmetric flows with swirl \cite{CSTY09,KNSS09,SS09} has been argued about but not measured.

This paper measures the growth that bears on the first and the quantities that decide the second. Its two halves are bound by one object: the table measures the growth of a family that lives on the front, and the theorem certifies an unstable eigenvalue of a parallel-flow model of that same front. The link is an identification, not an implication, and Section~\ref{sec:columnar} measures how far it holds -- the model brackets the two-dimensional rate rather than predicting it. Its contributions are, in order of weight:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{A certified unstable eigenvalue of a columnar model of the front} (Sections~\ref{sec:krawczyk} and \ref{sec:stageb}). For the parallel-flow problem on an explicit rational field we verify, in interval arithmetic with rigorous floating-point error bounds, an eigenvalue of the collocation pencil (Theorem~1); and by an argument of Plum's type for non-self-adjoint eigenvalue problems \cite[\S 9.3]{NPW19} -- a certified defect for a Galerkin eigenpair, a certified bound on the inverse of the shifted operator on the complement of the Galerkin space, and a Newton-Kantorovich fixed point -- we prove that the \emph{continuous} columnar operator has an eigenvalue of growth rate at least $\sn{5.080293}{4}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, that is $1.2435$ times the collapse rate of the state it is taken from (Theorem 2). Rigorous instability for a swirling column with axial flow is not new: Albritton and Ozanski \cite{AO25} construct the Leibovich-Stewartson ring modes of the inviscid column $V(r) e_\theta + W(r) e_z$ rigorously, with $O(1)$ growth rates in the joint large-wavenumber limit, and deduce nonlinear instability. What is new here, to our knowledge, is the form of the statement: a verified enclosure of a specific unstable eigenvalue of a \emph{viscous} such column, at a finite wavenumber, on an explicit field, with a rigorous radius. The weight is carried by the word verified. Verified enclosures of unstable eigenvalues in viscous parallel-flow stability do exist for the scalar Orr-Sommerfeld operator \cite{LP04,WPN09,BLMTW10} -- the last of these with exclosures as well, and with an eigenvalue proved to lie in the unstable region at $R = 5772.221818$, which is more than we claim here. Unstable modes of viscous swirling columns have of course been computed, and computed in three dimensions and in a pipe; what we have not found is a three-component swirling system with axial flow whose unstable eigenvalue is enclosed with an error bound a reader can check. The nearest verified eigenvalue in three-dimensional incompressible stability that we know of is that of Hou, Wang and Yang \cite{HWY26}, who certify an unstable eigenpair for the operator linearized about a self-similar Leray-Hopf profile, and deduce nonuniqueness from it; their object is a profile of the full equations rather than a column. Concurrently with this work, Dahne and Sverak \cite{DS26} certify an unstable eigenvalue of the linearization about a forward self-similar profile of the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, a scalar problem posed with the Navier-Stokes non-uniqueness question in view. It is a statement about that model, on that field, and about nothing else; Section~\ref{sec:stageb} says so precisely.
\item \emph{A non-axisymmetric stability table for Hou's collapsing state} (Section~\ref{sec:table}): growth rates of azimuthal modes $m = 0, 1, 2$ about the Euler and the viscous state, at three viscosities, with resolution pairs where they exist, the dependence of the crossing on viscosity, and the identification of the family that carries the instability as a short-wave band on the front. To our knowledge this is the first non-axisymmetric stability computation of this scenario, and we have found none for any other axisymmetric blowup candidate.
\item \emph{The nonlinear fate of the unstable mode} (Section~\ref{sec:nl}): on the Euler states the mode depletes the collapse; on the viscous state, for the one localized seed run, the collapse is unaffected to 0.02 percent out to 24 percent of the remaining time and to within 0.15 percent out to 35 percent, and no run reached either a continued or an arrested symmetry-broken collapse.
\item \emph{A resolved first-stage viscous continuation and its constants} (Section~\ref{sec:cont}), including the identification of the front as a fed strained layer at the Burgers scale, and the end of the one-scale regime near the label x400.
\item \emph{The measurement against the exclusion theorems} (Section~\ref{sec:theorems}), with the observation that the quantity usually quoted, $\sup|u|\,|x'|$, is pinned from below by a circulation that obeys a maximum principle and is attained in an outer flow that is effectively frozen over the window, so that the informative quantities are the core meridional ones, $|r u^r|$ and $|r u^z|$.
\end{enumerate}

A distinction that the events of September 2026 make necessary. Finite-time blowup has been claimed for the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with a smooth force compactly supported in space and time \cite{OAI26a}, for the unforced Euler equations from smooth compactly supported data \cite{OAI26b}, and, in the same week, for forced Euler, Boussinesq and porous-medium flows \cite{AB26}, continuing the multiscale programme of Cordoba and Martinez-Zoroa \cite{CM23}. A force of that kind satisfies Fefferman's conditions (4) and (5), so a correct proof of the first would settle option (C) of the Clay problem \cite{F00}. None of these claims had been independently verified as we wrote -- the Lean development accompanying \cite{OAI26a} records itself as self-assessed, and the one accompanying \cite{AB26} as verified by an author; since then the former has added a harness for checking its statements against an independently authored formalization of the Clay alternatives, which we note without having run it -- and none of them speaks to the object of this paper: Hou's scenario is unforced, and the exclusion theorems we measure against \cite{CSTY09,KNSS09,SS09} are theorems about the unforced equation, which no forced construction tests. The mechanism those constructions use is, however, the same short-wave amplification that our table finds on this state, and Section~\ref{sec:obstruction} says what our measurements do and do not imply for it.

The paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:eqs} gives the equations, the solvers, their validation, and -- in Remark 1, which governs every rate in the paper -- the sense in which a perturbation outruns a collapse. Section~\ref{sec:table} is the stability table and the spectrum it is drawn from. Section~\ref{sec:cert} is the certificate: the columnar model of the front, the enclosure of its collocation pencil, and the enclosure of the continuous operator. Section~\ref{sec:nl} is the nonlinear fate. Section~\ref{sec:cont} is the continuation. Section~\ref{sec:theorems} places the measured quantities against the theorems. Section~\ref{sec:disc} discusses what the results mean for constructions of Type II singularities and for the regularity side.

\section{Equations, codes and validation}
\label{sec:eqs}

\subsection{Formulation}

We work with the Hou-Li variables
\[
u_1 = \frac{u^\theta}{r}, \qquad \omega_1 = \frac{\omega^\theta}{r}, \qquad \psi_1 = \frac{\psi^\theta}{r},
\]
on the periodic cylinder $\Omega = \{r \le 1,\ z \in [0,1)\}$, in which the axisymmetric Navier-Stokes equations read
\begin{align}
\partial_t u_1 + u^r \partial_r u_1 + u^z \partial_z u_1 &= 2 u_1 \partial_z \psi_1 + \nu \Delta_3 u_1, \label{eq:u1}\\
\partial_t \omega_1 + u^r \partial_r \omega_1 + u^z \partial_z \omega_1 &= \partial_z\!\left(u_1^2\right) + \nu \Delta_3 \omega_1, \label{eq:om1}\\
-\Delta_3 \psi_1 &= \omega_1, \label{eq:psi1}
\end{align}
with
\[
\Delta_3 = \partial_r^2 + \frac{3}{r}\partial_r + \partial_z^2, \qquad
u^r = -r\, \partial_z \psi_1, \qquad u^z = 2 \psi_1 + r\, \partial_r \psi_1 .
\]
The data are Hou's \cite{H23a,H23b},
\[
u_1(0, r, z) = \frac{12000\,(1 - r^2)^{18} \sin(2 \pi z)}{1 + 12.5 \sin^2(\pi z)}, \qquad \omega_1(0, r, z) = 0,
\]
odd and $1$-periodic in $z$, with the pole conditions $\partial_r u_1 = \partial_r \omega_1 = \partial_r \psi_1 = 0$ at $r = 0$.

\emph{The wall, where our problem differs from Hou's.} Hou imposes a no-slip no-flow condition at $r = 1$: in these variables $\psi_1(t,1,z) = 0$, $u_1(t,1,z) = 0$ and $\omega_1(t,1,z) = -\partial_r^2 \psi_1(t,1,z)$ enforced together with $\partial_r \psi_1(t,1,z) = 0$ \cite[eqs. (2.4)-(2.5)]{H23b}. Our solver imposes the no-flow condition $\psi_1(t,1,z) = 0$ alone; $u_1$ and $\omega_1$ are advanced at the wall with one-sided stencils and no boundary value, so the wall here is impermeable but not no-slip. The difference is a boundary effect at $r = 1$ on a structure that lives at $r \lesssim 0.03$ and collapses toward the axis; it is invisible in the checkpoint comparisons of Section~\ref{sec:gates} at the precision quoted there, and we have not attempted to quantify it further. Every statement below is a statement about the flow our solver computes.

The base solver (\texttt{axiphys}) integrates \eqref{eq:u1}-\eqref{eq:psi1} on a radial sinh-type map and an axial map, with the exponential filter of Hou and Li \cite{HL07}, a moving radial map that follows the collapse, and, for the runs of Section~\ref{sec:cont}, a front-following axial map described there.

\subsection{Azimuthal-mode solvers and what is measured}

A perturbation of azimuthal wavenumber $m$ about an axisymmetric base $U$ is written $v(r, z, t)\, e^{i m \theta}$ and obeys the linearized Navier-Stokes system
\begin{equation}
\partial_t v + (U \cdot \nabla) v + (v \cdot \nabla) U + \nabla q = \nu \Delta v, \qquad \nabla \cdot v = 0,
\label{eq:lin}
\end{equation}
with $\nabla$, $\Delta$ and $\nabla \cdot$ carrying the factor $i m / r$ in the azimuthal slot. We compute \eqref{eq:lin} in three ways. The frozen-base solver (\texttt{axi3dlin}) linearizes about a fixed snapshot and integrates the mode with an exact discrete pressure projection (the divergence-of-gradient operator assembled from the same difference stencils, banded, with a Neumann wall row so that the projected radial velocity vanishes at the wall) and the parity rules $v_r, v_\theta \sim r^{m-1}$, $v_z, q \sim r^m$ at the axis; viscosity enters through the combinations $v_r \pm i v_\theta$, which obey the Laplacians of index $m \pm 1$. The tangent-linear solver (\texttt{axi3dtl}) marches the nonlinear axisymmetric base and the mode in one Runge-Kutta step, linearizing about the instantaneous base at every stage, with the base's moving radial map installed as a fixed map and mapped bases transferred by exact sine series. The nonlinear solver (\texttt{axi3dnl}) carries modes $m = 1$ to $M - 1$ with the azimuthal convolutions evaluated pseudo-spectrally on $3M$ points and feeds the $m = 0$ Reynolds stress back into the base equations. For $m = 0$ the seed exponents become $v_r, v_\theta \sim r$ and $v_z \sim 1$, and the axial-mean Neumann problem for the pressure is singular and is pinned at the axis.

Two numbers are reported for every run. The first is the energy growth rate
\begin{equation}
E(t) = \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 \left(|v_r|^2 + |v_\theta|^2 + |v_z|^2\right) r\, dr\, dz, \qquad
\sigma(t) = \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{d \log E}{d t},
\label{eq:sigma}
\end{equation}
quoted throughout in collapse units as $\sigma\,(T - t)$, where $T$ is the fitted singular time of Section~\ref{sec:fit}. The second does not involve $T$ at all:
\begin{equation}
\lambda = \frac{d \log\!\big(E^{1/2} / a_b\big)}{d \log A}, \qquad
a_b^2 = \int_{\mathcal{B}} |U|^2\, r\, dr\, dz, \qquad A = \max |u_1|,
\label{eq:lambda}
\end{equation}
with $\mathcal{B}$ the co-moving core box $r < 3R$, $|z - Z| < 3Z$ about the swirl maximum $(R, Z)$. Since $A \sim (T-t)^{-1}$ to the accuracy of Section~\ref{sec:fit}, $\lambda > 0$ means that the perturbation's energy norm grows faster than the base's energy norm on the collapse scale, that is, that the perturbation outruns the collapse in that ratio. We report $\lambda$ cumulatively, from the start of each run.

\subsection{Gates}
\label{sec:gates}

Solid-body rotation is neutral to $\sn{1}{-10}$ in the frozen solver. On a Rayleigh-unstable column $V = r(1-r^2)$, $k = 2\pi$, an independent one-dimensional primitive-variable eigensolver reproduces the reference $m = 0$ growth rate (0.3708 against 0.370756, the latter computed independently here and not taken from the literature) and gives $\omega = 0.2481 + 0.3371 i$ for the physical $m = 1$ mode, a second mode at 0.446 being wall-localized and spurious. The frozen solver, seeded in the unstable annulus, approaches that eigenvalue from above rather than reproducing it: its rate peaks at 0.388 and decays monotonically to 0.363 at $t = 6$ against the eigensolver's 0.3371, the gap closing as the subdominant modes at 0.157 and 0.107 die out. An earlier version of this gate locked onto a wall artefact, which is why the wall row of the pressure projection is a Neumann row. The nonlinear code with a seed of $\sn{1}{-6}$ reproduces the tangent-linear rate to 1.3 percent (0.158 against 0.160) and generates the $m = 2$ harmonic at second order. Perturbations preserve the subgroup structure of their azimuthal wavenumbers exactly (a base carrying only even modes never generates an odd one; measured at $\sn{6}{-17}$), which is the elementary equivariance of \eqref{eq:lin} under rotation by $2\pi/p$ and is used below only to read the harmonic content of the nonlinear runs.

The base solver reproduces Hou's published checkpoints: the Euler vorticity ratio at his first checkpoint to one percent and the Navier-Stokes ratio to three percent at his checkpoint $t = 0.0022616$ (his Appendix A.2), where he reports 139.6 (the snapshot we use as a base is the neighbouring computed state at $t = 0.0022620220$, at which our vorticity amplification is 144.1; Table~\ref{tab:states}). The tangent-linear and frozen-base rates are compared on a common convention, the raw rate in inverse seconds at equal fraction of the remaining time: the two solvers normalize by different remaining times (the frozen one by the remaining time at the snapshot, the co-evolving one by the remaining time at the current time), so their printed columns are not comparable and a ratio taken between them is not a growth-rate ratio. On the common convention the co-evolving Euler $m = 1$ rate exceeds the frozen one by 4 percent at 2.2 percent of the remaining time and by 13 percent at 13 percent, and the excess then grows (Section~\ref{sec:euler}); they agree to within 4 percent only over the first 6.5 percent of the remaining time, where the base has not yet moved.

\emph{Amplification labels, defined exactly.} Two different labels are in use and we state both, because they are neither equal nor proportional. States of the Euler and first-stage Navier-Stokes solutions used as bases in Section~\ref{sec:table} are named by the amplification of the full vorticity maximum, $\max|\omega|(t) / \max|\omega|(0)$, which is how Hou identifies his checkpoints: `the x144 state' is his, and we reproduce 144.1 on it against his tabulated 139.6. The continuation of Section~\ref{sec:cont} and the series of Section~\ref{sec:theorems} are indexed instead by
\[
\text{(label)} = \frac{\max |u_1|(t)}{12000},
\]
the maximum of the swirl variable in units of the coefficient of the initial datum. That coefficient is not the initial maximum: $\max |u_1|(0) = 3266$, so a label of 331 is an amplification of $\max|u_1|$ by a factor 1216. We keep these labels because every log and every archived snapshot carries them, and we write them as `x331' to distinguish them from amplifications. Table~\ref{tab:states} gives both labels, with the times, for every state used below.

\subsection{The trivial directions and the threshold}
\label{sec:thresh}

On a Type I base $u = (T - t)^{-1/2} U\!\left(x / \sqrt{T - t}\right)$ the pointwise amplitude rate, in units of the collapse rate $1/(T-t)$, is $3/2$ for the time-translation direction $\partial_t U$ and $1$ for an axis translation, and a perturbation outruns the collapse pointwise -- the ratio $\|v\|_\infty / \|u\|_\infty$ grows -- when its pointwise rate exceeds $1/2$. What we measure is the energy rate \eqref{eq:sigma}, and the two are related in one direction only.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Remark 1 (the threshold in the energy norm).} \emph{On the bounded cylinder $\Omega$, $\|v\|_{L^\infty} \ge |\Omega|^{-1/2} \|v\|_{L^2}$. Hence if $\sigma\,(T - t) \ge 1/2 + \epsilon$ on an interval with $\epsilon > 0$, then $\|v\|_{L^2} (T-t)^{1/2}$ grows there like $(T-t)^{-\epsilon}$, and since $\|u\|_\infty (T-t)^{1/2}$ is bounded on a Type I base -- applied to the computed state this hypothesis is the measured constant of Section~\ref{sec:consts}, flat to eleven percent over the resolved range -- $\|v\|_\infty / \|u\|_\infty$ grows. The condition $\sigma\,(T-t) > 1/2$ is therefore sufficient for outrunning, whatever the perturbation's support does. It is not necessary: for a perturbation co-scaling with the collapse, whose support shrinks like $(T-t)^{3/2}$ in volume, the energy rate is the pointwise rate less $3/4$, so the symmetry directions sit at energy rates $1/4$ (translation) and $3/4$ (time translation) and the outrunning threshold at $-1/4$.}

\medskip\noindent We therefore use $\sigma\,(T-t) > 1/2$ as a \emph{conservative} criterion: every crossing fraction reported below is the point at which that sufficient condition is first met, not the point at which outrunning begins, and a family below it is not thereby stable. Where a verdict depends on the difference we report $\lambda$ of \eqref{eq:lambda}, which involves neither $T$ nor the pointwise normalization, and we compare each family with the symmetry directions of its own azimuthal wavenumber: for $m = 0$ these are the translation and the time translation, at energy rates $1/4$ and $3/4$; for $m = 1$ the axis translation, at $1/4$; for $m \ge 2$ there is none. For $m = 1$ the axis-translation field $-\partial_x U$ is an exact solution of the interior equations \eqref{eq:lin}, admissible up to a boundary term at $r = 1$, where it has a nonzero radial component because the cylinder is not invariant under translation; the term is negligible for a structure at $r \lesssim 0.03$ and is projected out with the energy inner product (exact for a normal operator; the overlap reaches 0.33 to 0.36 in the long-wave runs and stays below 0.06 in the random-seed runs, so the projection is exact to about ten percent in the worst case); for $m = 0$ the overlap with $\partial_t U$ starts at 0.11 and falls monotonically to 0.07. We report both the raw rate and the rate of the orthogonal part where it matters.

A floor is known for the inviscid problem and we state its scope precisely, because it is often quoted more widely than it holds. For a Type I Euler blowup, Vasseur and Vishik \cite{VV20} bound the growth of the linearized \emph{Euler} semigroup below by the vorticity amplification, which for a Type I blowup implies a Lyapunov exponent of at least $1/2$ in these units, and Lafleche, Vasseur and Vishik \cite{LVV21} prove an axisymmetric counterpart, in weighted $L^p$ and under an extra hypothesis on the datum, with a $p$-dependent rather than a universal threshold. Both realize the growth with short-wave packets on bicharacteristics, so the class is identified even though no concrete or spectral mode is, neither bounds how far above it they lie, and neither applies to the viscous linearization, in which short waves are damped at rate $\nu k^2$. For the viscous states of Sections~\ref{sec:ns4}-\ref{sec:cross} no such floor is known, and the inviscid value serves only as a reference.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Remark 2 (collapse units carry the error in $T$).} \emph{If a rate $q$ is quoted in units of $1/(T-t)$ and $T$ carries an uncertainty $\delta$, the quoted value is $q\,(1 + \delta/(T-t))$ to first order.} On the state of Sections~\ref{sec:ns4}-\ref{sec:columnar}, $\delta/(T-t) = \sn{1}{-7} / \sn{2.4478}{-5} = 0.41$ percent, and every collapse-unit number quoted for that state carries that relative uncertainty in addition to its own. For the Euler states no fitted $T$ exists (Section~\ref{sec:euler}) and the band is much wider.

\subsection{Resolution checks}
\label{sec:res}

Every long-wave entry on the frozen Euler base has three axial resolutions (512, 1024 and 2048 points, with the localized seed pinned at the same position) and a radial pair (an exact subsample of the sinh-map grid to 257 points against 513). The short-wave families have an axial pair (1024 against 2048) on the viscous base, at 3.9 and 5.2 percent of the remaining time. The fastest-growing co-evolving run has an axial pair of its own, 512 against 1024 on the same base exactly re-gridded, which agrees over the first 5 percent of the remaining time and then separates to a factor 1.4 by 22 percent: the threshold crossing of Remark 1 is reproduced to 0.1 percentage points, the late magnitudes are not, and we say so where they are used (Section~\ref{sec:table}). The other late co-evolving values, at 23.9 to 34.2 percent, have no pair at all, and neither does the twinned run beyond 22 percent. The viscous continuation has a twin at a different axial map and Courant number, and the front-resolved runs have two maps. Three earlier readings were retracted during the work and are recorded as such in the supplementary record: a fit-dependent departure of the Type I constants (the singular-time degeneracy of Section~\ref{sec:fit}), a grid-scale event in a seeded run at the x200 state, and a three-cell front thickness.

\section{Non-axisymmetric stability of the collapsing state}
\label{sec:table}

\subsection{Conventions, and the two Euler caveats}
\label{sec:euler}

The states are those of Table~\ref{tab:states}. Collapse units on the viscous branch use the fitted $T = 0.0022865$ of Section~\ref{sec:fit}; the runs themselves were integrated with the Euler checkpoint value $T_{\mathrm{est}} = 0.002278$ as the normalizing time, and the viscous entries below are the same measurements renormalized to the fitted $T$.

On the Euler branch there is no fitted singular time and we do not invent one. Running the log-derivative method of Section~\ref{sec:fit} on our densest Euler record (a $513 \times 512$ run with twenty-six retained snapshots to $t = 0.0022736$) does not converge: the last seven four- and five-point windows give $T$ between 0.0022716 and 0.0022845 with the exponent drifting from 0.905 to 1.35, and neither stops moving as the window slides toward $T$, so Luo and Hou's criterion is not met; a separate Euler run passes $t = 0.002278$ with an amplitude of $\sn{1.5}{6}$, still finite. Collapse units on the Euler branch therefore use $T_E = 0.002278$, Hou's checkpoint, and carry a systematic band: over the range of admissible $T$ the frozen-base entries move by about $\pm 9$ percent and the late co-evolving ones by about $\pm 17$ percent. Every Euler number below should be read with that band attached, and the Euler conclusions rest on ratios -- between resolutions, between azimuthal wavenumbers, between the frozen and the co-evolving base, and between the two-dimensional and the columnar rate -- each of which is taken at equal time and is invariant under the choice of $T$.

\subsection{The table}
\label{sec:ns4}

Table~\ref{tab:spectral} is the paper's central measurement. Each row is one tangent-linear or frozen-base run: the fraction of the remaining time at which the energy rate $\sigma\,(T-t)$ of \eqref{eq:sigma} first meets the conservative criterion of Remark 1; the fraction at which it exceeds the symmetry directions of its own azimuthal wavenumber ($3/4$ for $m = 0$, $1/4$ for the translation-orthogonal part at $m = 1$, none for $m \ge 2$); the last measured value and the fraction at which it is taken; and the cumulative $\lambda$ of \eqref{eq:lambda}, which involves no fitted time.

\emph{How to read the $\lambda$ column.} The core box of \eqref{eq:lambda} is built on the grid location of the swirl maximum, whose axial index moves by whole cells; when it steps, the box height jumps by 13 percent (Euler) to 30 percent (viscous) and puts one step into the cumulative $\lambda$. Exactly one such step occurs in each run, and we give $\lambda_{\mathrm{cum}}$ as a bracket whose upper end is the logged value and whose lower end has that step removed. The truth lies between. Where the bracket does not straddle the relevant threshold the sign verdict is safe, and where it does we say so. Early cumulative values are meaningless (at the first output $\log(A/A_0) \approx 0.008$, so a half-percent change in the base norm moves $\lambda_{\mathrm{cum}}$ by 0.6); only the last third of each run gives a usable value. The two diagnostics are consistent: for a Type I base $\lambda = (\sigma (T-t) + 1/4)/p$, which reproduces the logged $\lambda$ to a few percent on every run.

\emph{What the table supports.} At Hou's first-stage viscosity every family tested meets the conservative criterion inside the first eleven percent of the remaining time, and the short-wave families of all three azimuthal wavenumbers meet it within half a percentage point of one another (4.2, 4.3 and 4.7 percent for $m = 2$, 1 and 0), which is a property of the sheet they live on and not of a symmetry class. Their last measured rates, 1.48, 2.15 and 2.08, are 3.0 to 4.3 times the conservative threshold, and each exceeds every symmetry direction of its own wavenumber; the cumulative ratios, $+0.66$ to $+1.49$ across their brackets, say the same thing without reference to $T$. The long-wave $m = 1$ direction, a displacement of the collapse, also clears both, ending at 1.176 with a translation-orthogonal part of 1.045. On the Euler state the excess is smaller, a factor 1.4 to 1.8, with cumulative ratios from $+0.55$ to $+0.93$ across their brackets, the long-wave $m = 0$ direction included.

Three qualifications belong with these numbers and are not decorations. First, the late co-evolving values are not converged in the axial resolution. The fastest-growing entry in the table, and the source of its headline value, has been repeated at half the axial resolution ($513 \times 512$ against $513 \times 1024$) on the same base state exactly re-gridded. The two agree to 8 percent over the first 5 percent of the remaining time and then separate steadily: the coarse run's rate is a factor 1.37 to 1.55 lower from 8 percent onward, and at the last fraction the two share, 21.6 percent, it gives $\sigma\,(T-t) = 1.26$ against 1.79 and a cumulative $\lambda$ of $+0.93$ against $+1.35$. Their axial wavenumber centroids separate with them, 114 against 183 cycles per unit, each about 40 percent of its own Nyquist in a run that carries no filter. Had viscosity selected the scale, the two would have settled on the same physical wavenumber; that they instead settle at a similar fraction of their own Nyquist says that the short end of the band is set by the grid. What survives this is the criterion the paper actually applies: both resolutions cross Remark 1's conservative threshold at the same time, 4.4 and 4.5 percent, and both keep $\lambda_{\mathrm{cum}}$ positive throughout. What does not survive is the magnitude: the crossings of $3/4$ and $1$ move from 5.7 and 7.6 percent to 8.1 and 17.2 percent, and the values quoted at 23.9 to 34.2 percent should be read as lower bounds that rise with axial resolution rather than as converged rates. A third axial resolution, which is what would decide whether they converge at all, has not been run. The twin also draws a different realisation of its random seed, so the comparison is not seed-matched; that the two agree early and diverge only as their wavenumber centroids diverge points to the resolved axial band rather than to the seed. The frozen pairs remain the rest of the resolution support, agreeing to 1.3 to 8 percent but only out to 14 to 26 percent of the remaining time. Second, the one Euler family that fails the conservative criterion, the long-wave axisymmetric direction, is not thereby stable: its rate peaks at 0.454 (co-evolving) and 0.495 to 0.497 (frozen, three axial resolutions, radial pair to 1 percent), which sits on the threshold inside the $\pm 9$ percent Euler band, while its cumulative $\lambda$ is strictly positive, $[+0.55, +0.73]$, so it outruns the collapse in the norm-consistent ratio, and lies between the two symmetry directions of its own wavenumber. An earlier draft of this paper called that direction stable; the statement the data support is that it clears neither the conservative threshold nor the time-translation direction at $3/4$, while exceeding the translation direction at $1/4$. Third, at the highest viscosity tested, $\nu = \sn{1}{-2}$, the two criteria disagree in sign: the rate clears the conservative threshold from 16.8 percent, while the cumulative ratio is negative throughout, $[-0.54, -0.09]$, the perturbation not yet having recovered its initial viscous decay. We report that as it stands.

Figure~\ref{fig:2} collects the viscous rates of this subsection and of Section~\ref{sec:cross}.

\emph{The families themselves.} The short-wave families are excited by a smooth random seed under the same envelope and live in a thin band on the front, with an axial wavenumber centroid that marches with the collapse and production dominated by the meridional shear. On the Euler state the frozen $m = 1$ family runs from 19.5 to 79.5 cycles per unit over its resolved range and the $m = 0$ family reaches 117; on the viscous state the co-evolving $m = 1$ family ends at 207, against an axial Nyquist of 512 in a run that carries no filter, which is the resolution caveat of Section~\ref{sec:res} in its sharpest form. For comparison the long-wave $m = 1$ direction on the Euler state, which is a displacement of the collapse rather than a band on the front, moves only from 6.9 to 35.0. This is the continuum Hou describes as the `shearing instability', which he reports as the strongest of the fluid dynamic instabilities that `typically occurs near the sharp front' and which, he states, a second-order vanishing numerical viscosity `would not be strong enough to suppress' \cite[Sec. 3.6]{H23a}. The long-wave $m = 1$ direction is a displacement of the collapse: its precession rate $\omega (T-t)$ passes from $+0.12$ through zero to retrograde near 40 percent of the remaining time, which the $SO(2)$ symmetry of a swirling base permits and which is not a bifurcation signature; the swirl share of its energy production rises from 0.07 to 0.47 and falls back to 0.37.

\subsection{The crossing fraction versus viscosity}
\label{sec:cross}

Applying a viscosity to base and mode from the x144 state -- which is a switch made at that state, earlier in the remaining time than Hou's own switch at $t_0 = 0.00227375$, and therefore not his second stage -- the fraction of the remaining time at which the $m = 1$ short-wave family meets the conservative criterion is 4.3 percent at $\sn{5}{-4}$, 5.2 at $\sn{1}{-3}$, 7.5 at $\sn{2}{-3}$, 14.5 at $\sn{5}{-3}$ and 16.8 at $\sn{1}{-2}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:3}). Over the decade from $\sn{1}{-3}$ to $\sn{1}{-2}$ the crossing fraction rises by 11.6 points, roughly linearly in the logarithm of the viscosity and flattening at the top. At every viscosity from Hou's first stage to twice his second, the family meets the criterion before a fifth of the remaining time has elapsed. We do not extrapolate the trend to a viscosity that would hold the family below the threshold for half the remaining time: the five points span a factor twenty in viscosity and any such extrapolation lands far outside them.

A remark on what the viscosity axis is, because these data invite a misreading. Hou's initial data have vanishing $\omega_1$, and for such data the system carries an exact scaling: the solution at amplitude $\lambda$ and viscosity $\nu$ is $\lambda$ times the solution at unit amplitude and viscosity $\nu/\lambda$, run at time $\lambda t$, so the two parameters enter only through their ratio and the amplitude of the initial swirl is not an independent knob. For data with $\omega_1 \neq 0$, such as the evolved states used here, the equivalence holds only if all fields are scaled together; a viscosity sweep on a fixed evolved base is then equivalent to a joint amplitude sweep of that base, and not to a swirl-only sweep. What this means for anyone varying Hou's setup is that only the lobe geometry and a nonzero initial $\omega_1$ are genuinely independent directions.

\subsection{An analytic cross-check}
\label{sec:ls}

Leibovich and Stewartson's sufficient condition \cite{LS83} for non-axisymmetric short-wave instability of a swirling flow -- whose ring modes Albritton and Ozanski \cite{AO25} have since constructed rigorously under their own hypotheses -- $\Phi = V\, D\Omega\,[D\Omega\, D(rV) + (DW)^2] < 0$ with $V$ the swirl, $\Omega = V/r$, $W$ the axial velocity and $D$ the radial derivative, is evaluable on the axisymmetric base alone. On the grid fields it is satisfied in a band just outside the swirl maximum on every state examined: at $(r, z) = (0.0264, 0.0088)$ against the maximum at $(0.0250, 0.0078)$ on the Euler x28 state, at $(0.0140, 0.0040)$ against $(0.0138, 0.0037)$ on the viscous x144 state, and at $(0.0029, 0.0009)$ against $(0.0029, 0.0008)$ at x222; the implied short-wave growth is of order the collapse rate. Rayleigh's centrifugal discriminant is negative on 6, 12 and 33 percent of the column through the swirl maximum inside twice its radius on the three states.

We attempted to make the same condition rigorous as a statement about an explicit polynomial field, by Sturm's theorem in exact rational arithmetic on a degree-20 Chebyshev fit of the column through the swirl maximum, and we withdraw the attempt. The criterion carries $D\Omega$ in its prefactor as well as inside its bracket, and the fit's first derivative is wrong by up to a factor of two near the swirl maximum, which is precisely where the annulus of interest lies; on the fitted field the quantity is negative only in a sliver at the outer edge of the fit, and interval arithmetic does not certify even that. An earlier version of this paper reported such a certificate. It rested on a misstatement of the criterion -- a prefactor $2V\Omega$, which is non-negative and therefore cannot invert the test where $\Omega$ decreases, and an axial term $D(W^2)$ in place of $(DW)^2$, which is not dimensionally homogeneous with the term beside it -- and it is retracted along with the code that produced it. The statement about the flow is the uncertified grid evaluation above, which is unaffected in its conclusion: recomputed with the criterion as Leibovich and Stewartson state it, $\Phi$ is still negative in a band just outside the swirl maximum on all three states, with the coordinates given there.

\subsection{The spectrum of the frozen operator, and why the enclosure is one-dimensional}
\label{sec:frozen}

The rates of Table~\ref{tab:spectral} are growth rates of evolved perturbations, not eigenvalues. A direct eigenvalue computation of the frozen $m = 1$ operator shows why the distinction matters. On the Euler x28 state at $257 \times 512$, shift-invert Arnoldi at $\sigma (T-t) = 3.0$ returns $\sigma (T-t) = 3.035$ and 1.096 (frequencies $-109.5$ and $-110.9$ in collapse units) with relative residuals $\sn{2.2}{-5}$ and $\sn{5.0}{-5}$, axial wavenumber centroids at half the resolved range and radial centroids just inside the swirl maximum: these are the short-wave shearing continuum at the grid scale, whose rate grows with resolution, and not the long-wave rate 0.3 to 0.5 that the localized seed excites. The long-wave direction is therefore not a leading discrete eigenvalue of the inviscid frozen problem, and an inviscid eigenvalue enclosure would be a statement about the grid.

The viscous operator damps the short waves and should have a resolution-convergent leading eigenvalue; that is the object a rigorous enclosure of the two-dimensional problem would target. Plain Arnoldi did not reach it: at $513 \times 1024$ the iteration failed to converge, and at $257 \times 512$ with a Krylov space of 60 it had not returned after 8.5 CPU-hours and was stopped. The leading eigenvalues sit in a cluster whose separation is of the order of the viscous damping of neighbouring short waves, which is the regime in which unshifted Arnoldi stalls \cite{MR96,LS01}. We tried both matrix-free remedies: Arnoldi on the propagator over 6.5 percent of the remaining time did not converge, and shift-invert with an inner GMRES solve stalled at a 36 percent inner residual for a real shift at the conservative threshold, with and without a shifted-diffusion preconditioner, which says that the shifted operator is nearly singular over a region -- the shift lies inside the pseudospectrum of the damped continuum rather than near an isolated eigenvalue. The leading viscous eigenvalue of the two-dimensional operator is therefore not isolated at this resolution, and this bounds what a rigorous enclosure of that operator could achieve, since every enclosure radius scales with the inverse of the distance to the continuum. The reachable rigorous statement is the one-dimensional radial problem on the front column, which is the subject of Section~\ref{sec:cert}.

\section{A certified unstable eigenvalue of the columnar model}
\label{sec:cert}

Before the model is described, why certify \emph{it}. Three reasons, and they are the reasons this section exists rather than one about the collapse itself. First, it is the only object here with an isolated eigenvalue to enclose, and Section~\ref{sec:frozen} establishes that rather than assuming it: the two-dimensional operator's leading eigenvalue is not isolated at any resolution we can run, and both matrix-free remedies stall inside the pseudospectrum of the damped continuum. Second, a swirling column with axial flow is a classical object in its own right, not an artefact of this scenario; its instability is the Leibovich-Stewartson mechanism, whose modes Albritton and Ozanski \cite{AO25} have constructed rigorously in the inviscid case. Third, the enclosure is a genuine computation -- a non-self-adjoint operator, a Galerkin space of dimension $7682$, and a certified Stokes spectrum underneath it -- and is a contribution to verified numerics independently of what it says about this scenario. What it is not is a statement about the front, and Section~\ref{sec:stageb} says so precisely.

\subsection{The columnar model of the front}
\label{sec:columnar}

A column of the flow at fixed height, treated as a parallel swirling flow $(V, W) = (r\Omega, W)$ with axial velocity, has normal modes $\exp(i m \theta + i k z - i \omega t)$ governed by a one-dimensional eigenvalue problem, which we solve by Chebyshev collocation with the axis conditions imposed by parity and no-slip at the outer edge of the fitted column ($r_{\max} = 2R$). The column that carries the instability is the front's, not the swirl maximum's. On the grid column through the front at the height where the two-dimensional $m = 1$ mode peaks, the columnar solver has an isolated unstable viscous $m = 1$ eigenvalue with growth 1.24 in collapse units at $kR = 28$ (converged in resolution and domain, 20 percent above the next eigenvalue, inviscid limit 1.27 to 1.36 and still rising slowly with $k$), against 1.21 to 1.24 for the frozen-base two-dimensional rate at 13 percent of the remaining time. The columnar rate varies from 0.78 to 1.61 across the front's thickness; the columnar eigenfunction sits at $1.3$ to $1.4R$ where the two-dimensional mode peaks at $1.0R$; and on the inviscid x28 state, whose front is sharper, no column reproduces the two-dimensional rate at all (columnar rates 0.4 to 0.7 against 0.92, at twice the radius). The parallel-flow model is therefore local: it supplies a candidate mechanism for the viscous front and brackets rather than predicts the two-dimensional rate. What it provides is a discrete, well-separated eigenvalue of a one-dimensional problem, which is the object a rigorous enclosure can reach.

Figure~\ref{fig:6} collects the columnar spectra of the front column against wavenumber, with the certified eigenvalues of Theorem 1 marked.

\emph{Mechanism.} On the front column the circulation $r^2\Omega$ decreases outward beyond $1.2R$, so Rayleigh's discriminant is negative on $1.21R$ to $2.0R$, and the inviscid $m = 1$ rate approaches the local centrifugal rate $\sqrt{-\Phi_R} = 1.47$ collapse units from below as $k$ grows (1.27, 1.34, 1.36 at $kR = 22, 44, 88$) with the eigenfunction narrowing onto the radius of the bound's maximum, which is the fixed-$m$ large-$k$ limit of Billant and Gallaire \cite{BG05,BG13}; the viscous peak at $kR = 28$ is the Mayer-Powell cutoff of that branch \cite{MP92}. The axial flow of the collapse extends the centrifugal instability to every azimuthal wavenumber \cite{BG13}, and on the front column the viscous columnar peaks are 1.21, 1.24, 1.22 and 1.16 collapse units for $m = 0, 1, 2, 3$, at $kR = 22, 28, 33$ and 44, all in the same annulus: one centrifugal instability of the front at every azimuthal wavenumber, not three. Without axial flow a Rayleigh-stable column is spectrally stable under further hypotheses \cite{GS20}. Two limits of this identification should be stated. The rate $\sqrt{-\Phi_R}$ is the large-wavenumber centrifugal limit and not a universal bound: under strong axial shear the Leibovich-Stewartson rate exceeds it, so approaching it from below is a property of this column. And in the two-dimensional runs the differential-rotation term supplies between nothing and 13 percent of the energy production of the viscous families, and under 9 percent over most of each run, the rest coming from the meridional shear, so the centrifugal identification is a statement about the columnar model and its eigenfunction, not a decomposition of the two-dimensional energy budget.

\subsection{A certified eigenvalue of the collocation pencil}
\label{sec:krawczyk}

We first certify the discretized columnar problem. Let $\Omega(s)$ and $W(s)$ be the degree-30 polynomials in $s = (r/r_{\max})^2$, $r_{\max} = 2R$, with exactly rational coefficients (the double-precision Chebyshev fit of the front column, converted exactly; the fit reproduces the grid column's eigenvalue to 0.01 percent), and let $(A_N, B_N)$ be the $N$-point Chebyshev-Gauss collocation pencil of the linearized viscous columnar problem on the field $(r\Omega, W)$, with no-slip imposed at the outermost collocation point $r_{\max}\cos(\pi/4N)$, axis conditions by parity, and every entry enclosed in interval arithmetic.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Theorem 1.} \emph{For $m = 1$, $k = 2000$, $\nu = \sn{5}{-4}$ and $N = 150$, the pencil $(A_N, B_N)$ has an eigenvalue in the disc of radius $\sn{1.2}{-7}$ about}
\[
\omega = -\sn{3.5051747}{4} + \sn{5.0850344}{4}\, i \quad \mathrm{s}^{-1},
\]
\emph{with an eigenvector in an explicit box in which the eigenpair is unique.}

\medskip\noindent The proof is a Krawczyk verification with rigorous floating-point error bounds (Rump's method \cite{R10}; midpoint-radius matrices; all products bounded by the classical $\gamma_n$ inequalities), and the code and its tests accompany the paper. The same verification at $N = 100$ gives radius $\sn{5.2}{-8}$ and agrees with $N = 150$ to nine digits, and at $N = 60$ gives $\sn{5.0850368}{4}$ with radius $\sn{2.4}{-8}$. An independent assembly of the pencil at 200 bits without the parity trick agrees with every stored entry within its radius, and a separate symbolic check reproduces the Cartesian linearized equations on a test field to $\sn{1}{-34}$. Three further certificates, each with radius below $\sn{1.3}{-7}$, are obtained at $N = 100$: at $\nu = \sn{5}{-3}$ with $k = 1200$, on the same $\nu = \sn{5}{-4}$ column with the viscosity of the operator replaced; for the inviscid problem at $k = 2000$; and for $m = 0$ at $k = 1600$, $\nu = \sn{5}{-4}$.

The enclosure is a statement about the eigenvalue in inverse seconds and does not involve the singular time; only the conversion to collapse units does, and by Remark 2 that conversion carries 0.4 percent. In collapse units the four certified growth rates are $1.245 \pm 0.005$, $1.008 \pm 0.004$, $1.300 \pm 0.005$ and $1.208 \pm 0.005$, that is 2.49, 2.02, 2.60 and 2.42 times the conservative threshold of Remark 1 -- as a comparison of scales only, since Remark 1's hypothesis is about a perturbation of the two-dimensional collapsing base, whereas the columnar operator is a frozen parallel flow with no singular time of its own, and the conversion borrows $T - t$ from the state the column is taken from.

What Theorem 1 certifies is that each of these four finite pencils, on an explicit rational field, has an isolated eigenvalue in the stated disc. It does not certify the continuous columnar operator -- that is Theorem 2 -- and it says nothing about the two-dimensional collapse, whose operator has no isolated eigenvalue to enclose (Section~\ref{sec:frozen}). The assumptions are those of every interval computation on BLAS and multiple-precision arithmetic: the real matrix product is a classical inner-product algorithm, the interval library is correct, overflow is detected and underflow is floored.
