\subsection{The front is a forced strained layer}
\label{sec:front}

The front's full width at half maximum is 0.087, 0.065, 0.063, 0.038, 0.029 collapse lengths $\sqrt{T - t}$ and 3.9, 2.9, 2.8, 1.7, 1.3 Burgers lengths $\sqrt{\nu (T - t)}$ from x131 to x268 (the first three grid-limited), and 1.0 Burgers lengths at x331 (six cells). The compressive strain at the front, measured on the symmetry plane at the ring radius and on the axis, is $a\,(T-t) = 2.2$ to 3.8. A Gaussian fit of the azimuthal vorticity across the front at x268 (24 cells inside three standard deviations) gives a standard deviation of $0.58 \sqrt{\nu (T - t)}$, a relative residual of 5 percent and a baseline of 9 percent of the peak; the strain implied by the thickness, $\nu (T - t)$ over the variance, is 2.9 against the measured 2.2 to 3.3; the velocity jump implied by the fit, $\sqrt{2 \pi}\, \delta\, \omega_{\mathrm{peak}} = 2600$, agrees with the measured jump of $u_r$ across the layer (2980) and with the integral of the vorticity (3240). The jump constant $\Delta U \sqrt{T - t}$ is 2.8 to 3.3, a third of the swirl constant. The sheet Reynolds number $\Delta U / \sqrt{\nu a}$ is 65 to 100 with the measured strain (120 to 150 if the nominal collapse strain $a = 1/(T-t)$ is used instead) and, under the Type I scaling, constant in time, so the shear family of Section~\ref{sec:ns4} is never frozen out. At x331 (six cells) the fit residual is 10 percent and the implied strain 5.5 against a measured 3.8, and the $u_r$ jump no longer accounts for the vorticity integral as the sheet tilts (the ratio of the radial to the azimuthal vorticity maximum rising from 1.1 to 2.1): the identification holds to the resolution available.

The front is therefore locally a Burgers-type strained layer: its profile is Gaussian and its thickness is $\sqrt{\nu / a}$ with the measured strain, which are the profile and the width of the Rott-Lundgren solution $u = (-a x, v(x,t), a z)$, $v_t - a x v_x = \nu v_{xx}$ (the planar strained layer of Burgers and Townsend; \cite{R58,L82} treat the axisymmetric core and the strained spiral) under the same strain. It is not that solution. In the Rott-Lundgren layer the velocity jump $\int v_x\,dx$ is conserved for any strain history, while the jump measured here grows like $(T-t)^{-1/2}$, by a factor of about 1.6 from x131 to x331; the layer here is fed, its jump supplied by the axisymmetric source of $\omega_\theta$ in \eqref{eq:om1}, which the free solution does not have. One consequence is worth stating, because it is the sheet-or-tube question asked of this scenario. If the front floors at one Burgers length -- which the series above shows only as a trend, its last point being six cells wide -- its thickness is $\sqrt{\nu(T-t)}$ while the collapse radius is $2.3\sqrt{T-t}$, so the front's thickness is $\sqrt{\nu} = 0.022$ collapse lengths and about one percent of the collapse radius -- and that ratio is then fixed, both lengths scaling as $\sqrt{T-t}$. The front stops flattening relative to the collapse rather than continuing to thin, so the collapsing object is a tube carrying a thin internal layer of fixed relative thickness, not a structure that is itself becoming a sheet. What the identification gives is the thickness law and the profile, and with them the statement that the front sits at the viscous scale $\sqrt{\nu (T-t)}$ rather than at the collapse scale: the vorticity's super-$1/(T-t)$ growth between x25 and x268 is its approach to that floor.

\subsection{The local $L^3$ norm}
\label{sec:l3}

The scale-invariant quantity $\|u\|_{L^3(B)}$, $B$ the ball of radius four collapse lengths $4\sqrt{T-t}$ about the axis point the ring converges to, was computed on the resolved snapshots from x4 to x268: 25.6, 25.3, 25.0, 24.6, 24.1, 23.3, 23.2, 23.1, 23.0, 22.8, 22.6, 22.5, 22.4, 22.3, 22.0, a monotone decrease of 14 percent over four units of $\log(1/(T - t))$, with the balls of eight and sixteen collapse lengths decreasing faster. What this does and does not say is stated in Section~\ref{sec:l3say}.

One snapshot of the series, at $t = 0.002285549$, is excluded from this and from every series in Section~\ref{sec:theorems}, and we state the exclusion and its ground here. Its axial map had degraded (Section~\ref{sec:map}), and it is anomalous in every diagnostic computed on it: the local $L^3$ norm reads 34.8 against a neighbouring trend at 22.0, and $\sup |u|\,|x'|$ reads 556 against 72. The twin run on a second map at the same instant reads 72.2 and continues the series smoothly. The excluded value is the largest in the series, so the series as quoted omits its largest value; it is a numerical artefact of one map, and we report it rather than let a reader discover a gap in the times.

\section{The scenario against the exclusion theorems}
\label{sec:theorems}

\subsection{What the theorems require}
\label{sec:hyp}

For axisymmetric flows with swirl the relevant exclusions are these. Chen, Strain, Tsai and Yau \cite{CSTY09} prove that axisymmetric strong solutions with swirl in $\mathbb{R}^3$ satisfying a Type I bound $|v| \le C_* |t|^{-1/2}$, with $C_*$ arbitrary, are regular, under their standing hypotheses on the data and the pressure. Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin and Sverak \cite{KNSS09} prove a Liouville theorem for bounded ancient axisymmetric solutions with swirl under the hypothesis
\begin{equation}
|v(x, t)| \le \frac{C}{|x'|}, \qquad |x'| = \text{distance to the axis},
\label{eq:H}
\end{equation}
and deduce regularity for solutions whose Leray rescalings inherit \eqref{eq:H} uniformly. Seregin and Sverak \cite{SS09} prove the local statement: on a parabolic cylinder about an axis point, an axisymmetric suitable weak solution with the bound \eqref{eq:H} \emph{on the meridional velocity} $\bar v = v_r e_r + v_z e_z$ is regular at that point. Singular points of an axisymmetric suitable weak solution lie on the axis: this follows from Caffarelli, Kohn and Nirenberg's $\mathcal{P}^1(S) = 0$ \cite{CKN82} together with the axisymmetric reduction stated in \cite[Sec. 3]{SS09}, a circle of singular points off the axis having positive one-dimensional measure. So the local theorem plus the localization of singular points is the step from a periodic cylinder to a statement about our flow, and no separate argument is needed. Barker \cite[Sec. 1 and footnote 3]{B25} makes the nearest prior observation: that Hou's solution appears to satisfy a Type I bound, that axisymmetric solutions satisfying such a bound cannot lose smoothness \cite{SS09}, and that this requires singular points to be excluded away from the axis, which for a no-slip cylinder needs boundary partial regularity \cite{SSS04} as well as \cite{CKN82}. Our wall is impermeable but not no-slip (Section~\ref{sec:eqs}), so that boundary result does not apply to the flow computed here; the collapse is interior and three orders of magnitude from the wall, and we claim nothing about wall points.

One structural remark decides what is worth measuring, and we state it because our own earlier reading of this point was wrong. In \eqref{eq:H} the swirl contributes $|v^\theta|\,|x'| = |\Gamma|$, the circulation, which for axisymmetric unforced flow obeys a maximum principle: it cannot exceed its initial value. The swirl part of the hypothesis is therefore satisfied automatically, for any such flow, and a measurement confirming it measures nothing. The content of \eqref{eq:H} is entirely in the meridional part,
\[
|x'|\,|\bar v| = \sqrt{(r u^r)^2 + (r u^z)^2},
\]
which is exactly the pair of quantities Hou names when he writes that the theorems apply `provided that $\|r u^r\|_\infty$ and $\|r u^z\|_\infty$ remain bounded for $r \ge r_0 > 0$' \cite[Sec. 1.4]{H24}. His gloss identifies the operative hypothesis correctly. What the theorems do \emph{not} require, and what a measurement of the global supremum of $|u|\,|x'|$ mostly reflects, is a bound on the full velocity in the outer flow.

\subsection{The measurements}
\label{sec:measure}

Every quantity in this subsection is independent of the fitted singular time.

\emph{The global quantity, and why it carries little information.} Recomputed from the archived snapshots (Table~\ref{tab:states}), $\sup_x |u(x,t)|\,|x'|$ reads 72.32, 72.23, 72.25, 72.29, 72.28, 72.24, 72.17, 72.19, 72.23, 72.15, 72.15, 72.13 on the twelve retained instants, from x9 to x329 (Table~\ref{tab:states} lists thirteen rows: x266 and x265 are two maps at one instant, and the series uses x266), over 3.3 units of $\log(1/(T-t))$: constant to 0.26 percent. A thirteenth is excluded on the ground given in Section~\ref{sec:l3}. Two facts limit what this shows. It is bounded below by the circulation maximum, since $|u|\,|x'| \ge |u^\theta| r = |\Gamma|$ pointwise, and $\max|\Gamma|$ falls only from 64.90 to 64.68 over the same states, pinned by its maximum principle; so nine tenths of the quantity is a number no flow of this class can change. And it is attained in the outer flow, at $r \approx 0.40$, $z \approx 0.09$ on every state, where $|u| \approx 180$ and the advective time $r/|u| \approx \sn{2.2}{-3}$, while the whole series spans $\Delta t \approx \sn{2.3}{-5}$, about one percent of one turnover of that flow. An outer maximum cannot move much over one percent of its own turnover whatever the core does; indeed the quantity still reads 72.08 on a snapshot past the fitted singular time. The measurement verifies that the hypothesis is not violated somewhere unexpected. It is not evidence about the collapse.

\emph{The core quantities, which are the informative ones.} In the core box $r < 3R$, $|z - Z| < 3Z$ of \eqref{eq:lambda}, over the same twelve states: $|u|\,r$ at the swirl maximum runs 21.1, 21.4, 21.6, 21.7, 21.6, 21.8, 21.7, 21.9, 22.1, 23.6, 21.8, 20.5, a spread of 16 percent with no trend, and a factor 3.3 below the global supremum; $|r u^r|$ is non-monotone, 19.1 at x9, falling to 14.9 at x72, and returning to 19.1 at x329; and $|r u^z|$ reads 7.5, 8.8, 8.9, 9.1, 9.2, 9.4, 9.5, 9.7, 9.9, 11.0, 10.3, 10.2, a rise of 36 percent from x9 to x329 that is not monotone: it peaks at 11.0 at x223, 47 percent above the start, and its last three values fall. Their global maxima, 49 to 64 for $|r u^r|$ and about 20 for $|r u^z|$, sit in the far field. The rise in $|r u^z|$ is the one trend in the operative pair over the resolved range, and it is not fast: against $\log(1/(T-t))$, which rises by 3.3 over the same states, it is a slope of about 0.9 per log-unit on a value of order ten.

\emph{Across the late transition.} The one-scale collapse ends near the label x400 (Section~\ref{sec:map}), and the ten snapshots of the wide-map run that bracket the transition, recomputed here on the same core box, carry the quantities across it. From x394 to x759, over 0.47 units of $\log(1/(T-t))$, the core $|r u^r|$ rises from 16.5 to 21.0, the core $|r u^z|$ from 9.9 to 15.8, and $|u|\,r$ at the swirl maximum from 21.9 to 23.7; at the two later snapshots, x917 and x905, $|r u^r|$ reads 22.4 and 21.7, above the band of 14.9 to 19.1 that holds over the whole one-scale range. The global supremum meanwhile falls from 72.07 to 71.94 and stays in the far field. So the operative quantities move upward, and substantially, exactly where the one-scale law fails. Over a quarter of a log-unit that is a jump between regimes and not a trend, no exponent can be fitted to it, and those snapshots are on maps past their tested contrast (Section~\ref{sec:map}); we report it because it is the only part of our data that reaches beyond the one-scale regime, and it moves in the direction an escape would need.

\emph{What this establishes.} Over the resolved range of the one-scale regime the computed first-stage solution satisfies the hypotheses of \cite{CSTY09,KNSS09,SS09}, with the constants above; a finite computation can establish membership in the excluded class only in that sense, since the hypotheses are bounds up to $T$. What it does not establish is any statement about the behaviour beyond that range, and the one place our data do reach beyond it, the transition, shows the operative quantities rising. The honest summary is that the scenario shows no departure over the range where it is a one-scale collapse, and that the data neither exhibit nor exclude the growth that an escape would need.

\subsection{Hou's escape and the log-weighted criteria}
\label{sec:escape}

The quantity Hou names as the escape is the global supremum of $|r u^r|$ in his generalized rescaled model \cite[Secs. 1.5 and 5.4.4]{H24}, reported to grow like $\log(1/(T - t))$ over amplifications from $\sn{1}{15}$ to $\sn{1}{30}$. His three-dimensional Navier-Stokes paper \cite{H23b} reports no value of it, and our range of amplifications has no counterpart in his: the comparison is structurally unavailable, and our data are inconclusive on it. We note only that a logarithmic law has an arbitrary offset, so the size of the rise it would produce over our range is not determined by the law alone, and that our measured core values are non-monotone over that range.

The log-weighted circulation criteria that appear in the same discussion, $\max |\log r|^{3/2} |\Gamma|$ and $\max (\log r)^2 |\Gamma|$ over $r < 0.1$, grow steadily in our run (163 to 223 and 314 to 486 over the earlier part of the continuation), as they must for a core of constant circulation collapsing toward the axis, since the weight itself grows. They are regularity criteria \cite{W16,LZ17}: their growth is necessary for a singularity, not evidence of one, and they are not measurements of the hypothesis of any exclusion theorem.

\subsection{A criterion that can be measured directly}
\label{sec:zhang}

A criterion posted while this paper was being written can be evaluated on our data, and we report the measurement because it goes against the scenario. Zhang \cite{Z26} proves that an unforced axisymmetric Leray-Hopf solution with bounded smooth data and bounded initial swirl times radius is regular provided the radial velocity satisfies a one-sided Type I lower bound, $u^r \ge -K/\sqrt{T-t}$. Violating that bound is therefore necessary for blowup in that class. We measure the smallest admissible constant, $K(t) = -\inf_x u^r \sqrt{T-t}$, on nineteen snapshots of the continuation. It stays between 5.05 and 6.29 over 4.58 units of $\log(1/(T-t))$ while the amplification rises 170-fold, with a least-squares slope of $-0.21$ per log-unit, that is slightly falling. The radial velocity itself grows ninefold over that range, from $-711$ to $-6496$: the flow becomes far more strongly inward, but at exactly the Type I rate and not faster. The infimum is attained in the core, on the inflow face of the front at 1.01 to 1.24 core radii, never on the axis and never in the outer region, on a feature spanning tens to hundreds of cells in each direction; the meridional Type I constant of Section~\ref{sec:consts} is this same inward jet. Three independent front-following maps agree to between 1 and 7 percent at matched instants and the two radial resolutions agree to four figures; perturbing the fitted singular time by its uncertainty leaves the sign of the trend unchanged, and only a perturbation a hundred times that size turns it positive, and even then $K$ reaches 8.7 rather than diverging. Two caveats attach: the criterion is a preprint and unrefereed, and our domain is a bounded periodic cylinder rather than $\mathbb{R}^3$, so the state is the natural analogue of the theorem's class rather than literally in it. Subject to those, the scenario does not escape through the quantity that criterion names.

\subsection{What the local $L^3$ norm does and does not say}
\label{sec:l3say}

The decrease of Section~\ref{sec:l3} contradicts no theorem as stated. The global conditions (a singularity requires the whole-space $L^3$ norm to blow up \cite{ESS03,S12}) say nothing about shrinking balls; Barker and Prange's logarithmic lower bound \cite{BP21} concerns balls of radius $(T - t)^{(1 - \delta)/2}$ with a doubly exponentially small constant; the at-scale theorems (Barker and Prange \cite[Thm. 2]{BP20}; Kang, Miura and Tsai \cite{KMT21}) are lower bounds by a small universal constant, and the measured 22, which is $\sn{4.4}{4}$ in the dimensionless units of those theorems, satisfies them by a wide margin. A Type I profile predicts the scaled norm to approach a constant, and a mild decrease toward a plateau is consistent with that. The sentence the data support is that the critical norm's content at the collapse scale is not growing, which is the opposite of the trend a singularity drives into the global critical norm: evidence against, not proof.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:disc}

\subsection{The continuum obstruction}
\label{sec:obstruction}

Constructions of log-corrected (Type II) singularities in parabolic and dispersive problems typically proceed from a stationary or self-similar profile of a limiting problem, its linearized spectrum with finitely many unstable directions, and a modulation argument; the compressible implosion programme of Merle, Raphael, Rodnianski and Szeftel \cite{MRRS22a,MRRS22b} is the model. For Navier-Stokes the limiting problem is Euler, viscosity being exactly marginal under the Leray scaling, and for the interior scenario this framing exists only as an exclusion programme \cite{BP20,BP21,S23}, never as a construction. Table~\ref{tab:spectral} measures the growth that such a construction would have to control about this state, and what it finds is not a finite list of unstable directions but a continuum: a short-wave family on the front, present at every azimuthal wavenumber tested, meeting the conservative criterion from 4 percent of the remaining time on the viscous state and 6 to 8 percent on the Euler state, and reaching 3.0 to 4.3 times that threshold by the last resolved point (a lower bound: the coarse axial twin of Section~\ref{sec:table} gives a factor 1.37 to 1.55 less). We identify that band with the essential spectrum of Lifschitz and Hameiri \cite{LH91}, Friedlander and Vishik \cite{FV91} and Vishik \cite{V96}, whose radius Vishik \cite{V96} identifies with the maximal Lyapunov exponent of the bicharacteristic amplitude cocycle; the identification is not something the measurement exhibits, the short end of the band being set by the grid (Section~\ref{sec:res}). Chen and Hou reconcile it with their stable boundary profile by working in a low-regularity weighted norm in which the outgoing transport damps short waves, declining the high-regularity estimate whose coercivity they call unclear \cite[Part I, Sec. 2.7.2]{CH25a}. A construction on the interior profile must either find such a norm or cut the continuum off with viscosity, and Section~\ref{sec:cross} says what viscosity does here: over a factor twenty it moves the crossing from 4 to 17 percent of the remaining time and removes it at no value tested.

A second obstruction is structural and explains why a self-similar description of this state resists both the one-scale and the two-scale ansatz. In the rescaled equations the aspect ratio of the two scales appears inside the elliptic operator, multiplying its radial part. A profile, being independent of the rescaled time, therefore requires that ratio to be constant, which forces the two similarity rates to be equal, which is to say one scale. We therefore see no route to a genuine two-scale fixed point of the unmodified equations, and state that as an observation about the rescaled equations rather than as a non-existence proof; a two-scale ansatz is available only if some extra degree of freedom pins the ratio, which is the role played by the space dimension treated as an unknown in \cite{H24}. Marching the dynamically rescaled two-scale equations from our own collapsing state, the rates neither converge nor drift steadily nor diverge: they make one excursion and return, at two resolutions agreeing to two percent. We record one reason the problem is hard to truncate. Deleting the vorticity outside the core removes at most four percent of the vorticity norm and a seventh of a percent of its source, yet moves the streamfunction on the swirl core by tens of percent, because the squared aspect ratio is of order $10^{-4}$ and the rescaled elliptic operator is therefore nearly one-dimensional in the axial variable, giving distant vorticity a long lever arm on the core. The collapse's own anisotropy makes its elliptic problem nonlocal, and no truncation that excludes the outer region is admissible.

\subsection{The unforced constructions of September 2026}
\label{sec:oai}

The same continuum is the engine of the constructions of \cite{OAI26a,OAI26b}, which amplify short waves on a background flow by the criteria of Lifschitz and Hameiri and of Friedlander and Vishik, and design the core to supply enough shear at its outer edge to amplify pulses placed there. In \cite{OAI26b} the mechanism runs unforced, on Euler, by iterating the amplification on successively shorter intervals, giving a gradient blowup with bounded velocity rather than a self-similar profile. So the family we identify as an obstruction to a self-similar unforced scenario is, used the other way, a route to a non-self-similar one, and our measurements bear on that route: an iteration of this kind compounds against the collapse when the rate in collapse units exceeds the conservative threshold, which on this state it does at every azimuthal wavenumber and by a factor of 3.0 to 4.3 at the last resolved point, itself a lower bound at the axial resolution we can run. We do not extrapolate that margin beyond the range over which it was measured.

What the measurement does not supply is the construction. Compounding is necessary for such an iteration and not sufficient: the iteration requires the shear amplified at one stage to be handed to the next, and that requirement is the whole of the gap between a forced construction and an unforced one. The force of \cite{OAI26a} is small in location rather than in norm -- it vanishes to infinite order at the singular point and is identically zero beyond a fixed scale -- and the flow already supplies the divergent part of its own force through the pulses' Reynolds stress; what remains external is that an exponentially small force seeds each pulse. In \cite{OAI26b} every seed of the iteration is placed in the initial datum at time zero, designed backwards and lying dormant until its stage activates, and what one stage hands to the next is the amplifier -- the shear, its frame and a coupling constant -- never the seed. Self-generation of seeds is neither claimed nor proved there. The question is not new: an iterated handoff of this kind was proposed for Navier-Stokes \cite{FH04} and shown not to work in the proposed form \cite{LL06}, the construction satisfying the equations only along a single trajectory and so being unusable as the background for the next iteration. It remains open for Euler and for positive viscosity, and these constructions avoid it rather than resolving it.

\subsection{What remains open}
\label{sec:open}

One line of pressure on the interior scenario is not ours and cuts against it. Every axisymmetric singularity must be faster than the scale-invariant rate \cite{CSTY08}, so its velocity exponent exceeds the Leray value; under the Euler scaling at an exponent above that value the swirl circulation carries a factor tending to zero, so the zoomed limit has no swirl \cite{S24}; and axisymmetric Navier-Stokes without swirl is globally regular \cite{L68,UY68}. The three steps do not compose into a theorem -- excluding the limit needs a decay hypothesis that is not proved, and holds only inside a parameter window -- but a reader who grants the decay hypothesis should conclude that the interior axisymmetric route is closed, and nothing we measure gives that reader a reason to reconsider.

It is worth saying where the measured exponents put this scenario on the one axis the exclusion literature parametrizes. With $R$ and $Z$ both scaling as $\sqrt{T-t}$ (Section~\ref{sec:consts}) and the amplitude exponent $p = 1.0 \pm 0.05$ of Section~\ref{sec:fit}, the swirl velocity $u^\theta \sim R\,A$ goes as $(T-t)^{-1/2}$: the collapse sits at the circulation-conserving Leray rate, to within the $\pm 0.05$ of the fitted exponent. That value is the extreme the bounds allow and not a point inside them. It is also the rate that the vortex-dynamics literature writes down directly: Moffatt's Leray scaling for a collapsing vortex pair, $u = \Gamma^{1/2}(t_*-t)^{-1/2}U(X)$, takes the conserved vortex strength itself as the amplitude \cite[eq.~(7.1)]{M00}, which is this exponent with circulation as its reason. Deng, Hou and Yu \cite{DHY06} note that Kelvin's theorem makes it the worst case for the velocity, and Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol \cite{CIV26} prove, for a nontrivial $C^2$ axisymmetric globally self-similar Euler profile with their decay hypotheses, that the zoom exponent is at least $1/2$, which is the same statement. The sharper reading is Chae and Shvydkoy's \cite{CS13}: for a locally self-similar Euler profile in $L^p \cap C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $3 \le p \le \infty$, the range that includes this exponent at $p = 3$ is excluded outright. So the rate we measure is the one that exact self-similarity in $L^3$ forbids, and the scenario's survival depends on its not being exactly self-similar -- which is what Section~\ref{sec:obstruction} finds independently, the aspect ratio drifting and the rescaled rates never balancing. The escape and the exponent are the same fact seen twice.

The most accurate self-similar profile for the axisymmetric Euler equations now available sits at the same place. Ganeshram, Duruisseaux and Anandkumar compute a single-scale profile, self-similar in $\mathring r/(T-t)^{1/2}$ and $(\mathring z - \mathring z_c(t))/(T-t)^{1/2}$ with the centre travelling along the symmetry axis, that is $\lambda = 1/2$ in their notation, the same rate as ours; they adopt that exponent for the certified profile, motivating it by the invariance of circulation and by \cite{CIV26}, and separately optimize the exponent jointly with the profile and find it converges near the same value \cite{GDA26}. Our measurement is of a different object -- a viscous continuation of a specific solution, not a profile -- and is a measurement rather than a construction, but it lands on the same exponent, and for the same stated reason.

Discretely self-similar and aperiodic Type I singularities are excluded only near the continuous case \cite{CW17a}, and in the axisymmetric swirl class every Type I singularity is excluded, so that loophole lives in the non-axisymmetric class, where the relevant computation -- a periodic or aperiodic orbit of the rescaled equations in three dimensions -- has never been attempted for a blowup problem; the closest precedent is Gundlach's computation of the Choptuik spacetime as a periodic orbit in similarity time \cite{G95}.

On the rigorous side of our own results, Theorem 2 certifies an unstable eigenvalue of the continuous columnar operator. Three things it does not do should be said once more here: it does not exclude other eigenvalues from the disc, it does not assert simplicity, and it says nothing about the front, the two-dimensional collapse or Navier-Stokes regularity, the columnar model being a parallel-flow approximation on an explicit polynomial field with an artificial wall. An enclosure for the two-dimensional operator is not reachable by the same route, because that operator has no isolated eigenvalue at the resolutions we can run (Section~\ref{sec:frozen}). Extending Theorem 2 to other wavenumbers is a matter of compute rather than of mathematics: nothing in the pipeline is wavenumber-independent, and each new $(m, k, \nu)$ needs its own certified Stokes spectrum, Galerkin matrix, strip norms and constants.

\subsection{Predictions for a three-dimensional computation}
\label{sec:pred}

No non-axisymmetric computation of Hou's data exists. The first one will test the following statements, which are the content of this paper reduced to numbers that a single run at $\nu = \sn{5}{-4}$, started from the axisymmetric solution at vorticity amplification 144 with a small random perturbation, can confirm or refute. A caveat first: our own symmetry-breaking run was repeated from an identical state on a grid with half the radial points, and the two agree to better than one percent on the collapse amplitude, on the maximum of the azimuthal velocity and on the ratio of the second azimuthal harmonic to the first, and to within half a percent at the last common time; the check does not speak to the axial direction, both runs carrying the same axial resolution, and the axial curvature width of the emerging structure is a small number of cells, so any statement here about axial contraction rates should be read as a statement about the grid until an axially refined pair is run.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The $m = 1$ energy in a thin band on the front grows, in the collapsing frame, faster than the conservative threshold from 4.3 percent of the remaining time ($\sigma (T-t) = 0.91$ at 6.7 percent, 1.29 at 11.4 percent), with $m = 0$ and $m = 2$ following at 4.7 and 4.2 percent, and all three exceed the collapse rate itself, at 7.5 ($m = 1$), 15.2 ($m = 0$) and 6.9 ($m = 2$) percent -- the $m = 1$ crossing moving to 17.2 percent at the coarser axial resolution, which makes it the weakest prediction here. The long-wave $m = 1$ direction crosses at 10.8 percent and reaches 1.18 by 34 percent. What is to be tested is the factor of 3.0 to 4.3 by which these families exceed the threshold at the last resolved point -- a lower bound, the coarse axial twin giving 1.37 to 1.55 less -- and which wavenumbers carry them.
\item The growth stays a distributed deformation of the ring, not a sub-vortex: the three-dimensional vorticity maximum reaches 1.7 times the axisymmetric one while the axisymmetric amplitude stays on its own law, 9 percent above the Type I line; the second harmonic stays at about two percent of the first; the mode's energy peaks on the ring at 0.98 of the swirl maximum's radius and 0.91 of its height with half-widths of 0.7 to 0.8 collapse lengths; no compact off-axis maximum forms at the viscous scale.
\item For a seed of relative size $\epsilon$ the symmetry breaking becomes order one after an amplification of at most $\epsilon^{-1/\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}}$ with $\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}$ between 0.68 and 1.65 on the viscous state, so a one percent seed reaches order one after an amplification of at most about 16 to $\sn{9}{2}$ of the amplitude at which it was introduced.
\item Applying $\nu = \sn{5}{-3}$ at the same state moves the crossing to 14.5 percent and the collapse rate to 19.2 percent (1.37 at 24 percent); the tenfold viscosity moves the crossing, it does not remove it.
\item Any resolved axisymmetric continuation of the $\nu = \sn{5}{-4}$ solution gives $\sup_x |u|\,|x'| = 72 \pm 1$ with no trend over 3.3 units of $\log(1/(T-t))$, a core value $|u|\,r$ at the swirl maximum of 20.5 to 23.7, the circulation maximum 64.7 to 64.9, the meridional Type I constant 5.3 to 6.5, an amplitude exponent $1.0 \pm 0.05$ jointly with a fitted singular time $0.0022865 \pm \sn{1}{-7}$ (the pair being correlated as in Section~\ref{sec:fit}), a front of thickness 1.0 to 1.7 Burgers lengths fitting a Gaussian to 5 percent, and $\omega (T-t)$ rising through 242 with a decreasing exponent.
\item On one map with the core window fixed in collapse units, the core-restricted $|r u^r|$ either stays within its present band of 15 to 19 or grows beyond x331; a resolved continuation to the label x1000 adds 1.1 units of $\log(1/(T-t))$ and decides between the two at the 10 percent level, which the present data cannot. Across the transition of Section~\ref{sec:map} the quantity rose from 16.5 to 21.0 in 0.24 log-units, above that band.
\end{enumerate}

A three-dimensional run in which the symmetry-broken state continues to collapse with its amplitude on the Type I law, or an axisymmetric continuation in which the core meridional quantities grow steadily beyond the resolved range, would refute the corresponding statement and with it this paper's reading of the scenario.
